sections.title: Kids learn from what you model
It's not on you to fix everyone

blocks.p: A parent wrote to me with a question about the flight and fight energy that comes up in parenting: how to keep it in check, and how not to pass it on to the next generation, our own kids. These are my general thoughts, not specific advice for this person or anyone else.
Here's what they wrote:

q: How does one who never really had models of calm, loving, safe parents learn to calm the inner storm of fight or flight brain that leads to angry yelling that then perpetuates the trauma cycle by scaring a little one? I know the science behind it, and I know the psychology, and I understand what's happening, but how do I stop/slow that reaction when my brain is hijacked?

blocks.p: There's a lot here, so let's take it one piece at a time.

blocks.h: Never having a model of good enough parenting

blocks.p: They said they never had models of calm, loving, safe parents. Let's just say good enough. We don't need perfection. We need good enough.

This is very common. How many of us had perfect parents? Probably zero. How many of us had good enough? I don't know. And when you look back, there was probably lots of room for improvement, even if you had good enough and came out into the world okay enough. Myself as a parent, there's lots of room for improvement, I think.

So some validation here. When we don't get the parenting we needed to thrive growing up, it makes it a lot more difficult to be the parent we want to be once we're ready to be parents. It lives within us, and it hinders us in some ways. Maybe less than good enough parenting can be an adversity that people build on, sure, but it can also be a hindrance.

We parent based on the way we were parented, unless you're actively learning new ways to parent and doing your own self-regulation practice to put them into action. That might mean perpetuating it, or it might mean saying, "I don't want to do this again with my own kids," and stopping it. Either way, it's the springboard for us as parents. And it can lead to a perpetuation of parenting dynamics that lasts for generations.

At the time, I worked with teenagers who typically had one parent in their life, usually a birth parent, and also grandparents. They were young enough to have two, maybe even three generations around them. And even as teenagers, they could see how the way they were being parented came from the way their parents were parented. They could see generationally how these things get passed on.

I have to keep an eye on myself too, just like anybody. I was raised in a home with a lot of yelling. Maybe that's part of an Italian kind of thing. Maybe. We yelled at each other constantly, and I always seemed to be in trouble and getting yelled at. So as a parent, I recognized early on that I had an impulse to yell, and that's something I have to keep in check. I do as much self-regulation as I can, and I do my own work, but that impulse to control and to yell is still in there. And I think it's not just me. A lot of us have these little impulses within us based on the way we were parented.

blocks.h: Aim for good enough, not perfect

blocks.p: Here's a reframe: don't worry about perfect parenting. Worry about good enough parenting.

That doesn't mean we're giving up, or settling exactly. If you have the mental space to worry about being a perfect parent, go right ahead. Good luck. But that might also be a defensive, impulsive thought: "I'm not good enough. I have to be perfect." If it comes from genuine self-improvement and you can handle it, cool. For the majority of people, worry about leveling up, day after day. Worry about good enough parenting.

blocks.h3: The larger scale: do better than your parents

blocks.p: Focus on improvement in a larger sense, generationally. Do better than your own parents. Just level up from them. If there was violence, we want to erase that entirely from our parenting. But at least do something better. Whatever the problem was with your parents that you can identify, cut that out.

ul: If your parents didn't say "I love you" at all, start saying it to your kids.
If your parents were good at saying it out loud but not very good at sharing love physically and affectionately, that might be where you level up.
If your parents weren't well regulated and had anger outbursts, that might be where you need to level up compared to them.

blocks.p: I know in mental health we say not to compare yourself to others. But as a reframe, I think it can help to look at it as "I am improving on what came before me." That's not an insult. It might be very practical.

blocks.h3: The smaller scale: do better than yourself yesterday

blocks.p: But you can't settle for just being better than your own parents. So also focus on improvement in a smaller sense, day to day. Do better than yourself yesterday.

Think about how you parented yesterday, and do better than that. Maybe you yelled at your kids on the way out of the house this morning. Next time, don't yell at them on the way out, or start getting ready earlier. If you were pressuring your kids to clean their room, threatening and yelling and name-calling, don't do that tomorrow. Maybe you still rush them a little, but cut out the name-calling. Level it up the next day as much as you can.

So we have the larger picture, generationally, and then the day-to-day improvements for yourself. Not perfection. We want to eventually get to good enough. Do better than your own parents, and do better than yourself as well. Challenge yourself.

Something else that can help is to create boundaries for acceptable parenting. If you have a husband, a wife, or a partner, talk about it with them, and maybe even agree: "We're not perfect people, but we can create boundaries for what's appropriate parental behavior."

I'd encourage everybody to base this on generally acceptable values of right and wrong. I'm not going to tell you the morality of your home. But hitting is wrong. Insulting children is wrong. Swearing isn't wrong, but in front of kids, maybe not. Yelling in and of itself isn't ideal with kids. These might be the boundaries for acceptable behavior for anybody in your home. But since change starts with the parents, I'd focus on yourselves first: here's what's right and wrong for us as parents. We're not perfect, but we can stop these things, or support each other in working toward stopping them.

If yelling and swearing is a problem for you, create that rule right now. This is just wrong. I don't want to treat anybody this way. I don't want to treat any children this way. And I really don't want to treat my children this way, because they're my kids, they need me, and yelling at them isn't going to help. Swearing at them and calling them names doesn't help at all. It makes things a lot worse.

So create that mental boundary of acceptable behavior for yourself, and actually enforce it. That's why talking with your significant other can help: you keep each other in check and support each other through it.

Prioritize not doing these things. Don't make it worse. It's not perfect, maybe not even good enough yet, but stop the cycle, because this is a generational thing. "I'm not going to yell." "I'm not going to name-call." "I'm not going to shame and blame." Maybe you don't know how to express love to your kids yet. You're not quite there. But you can stop swearing in front of your kids. That's doable. You can stop spanking your kids. Please. That cannot be allowed in the home. No hitting of any kind. It's not okay to hit kids.

blocks.h: Notice your wins, and share them

blocks.p: As you do this successfully, which you will, stop and notice those wins, and give yourself a little credit. Share them with somebody. Hopefully you've talked about this with someone, and you can say, "Hey, I did it," or, "We did it, and here's what went well." Don't keep it to yourself. Share, brag. If you're in a parenting group, share it with them, or with people online, or whatever you do to connect with other people. That helps solidify the progress you're making.

Take a moment to reflect on it: "You know what? I did better than yesterday. My amount of yelling was cut in half. It's not quite good enough, but it's a lot better than it was, so I'm giving myself a W for that, and I'm going to build on it tomorrow."

Especially if positivity was in short supply for you growing up, you have to be the one to grow it for yourself now. That's pretty common among the people I work with in therapy. Sometimes there just isn't a lot of positivity to go around, and your own parents weren't giving it. If that's your case, that sucks, and that's true. But it's also true that you can give it to yourself. As you get these little wins and improvements, you can give yourself some credit and say, "I can do this. I am doing this, and I can do even better tomorrow."

blocks.h: Expand what you know about parenting

blocks.p: I'd also encourage you to learn new parenting skills and new parenting paradigms. Expand your knowledge of what's possible. We parent the way we were parented, unless we have a bigger concept of what parenting is, what it looks like, and the different interventions out there. I think self-regulation is a big part of it.

That way, when those moments come up where you might default to generational parenting patterns, the new idea might pop into your mind, especially if you're self-regulated enough to put it into action.
One quick tweak to the question. They wanted to calm the inner storm of the "fight or flight brain." This isn't a brain issue. It's a whole body issue. It's a nervous system issue.

Very specifically, it's a brainstem issue, and that gets sent down to the body and up to the rest of the brain. We hear about the brain so much in mental health, and yes, it's important, I get it. But there are messages going from the body to the brainstem and messages going from the brain down to the brainstem. We say brain to body and body to brain, but really we mean messages to the brainstem in particular. The entire body is prepared for safety or for defense.

Here we're talking about defense. When we're yelling, when we're fighting, when we're being dominant and controlling and aggressive, that's fight state stuff. In fight, we're not increasing space. We're decreasing it. We're getting closer to the danger in order to get that danger to back off.

So we have to calm the body, and we do that by increasing cues of safety and creating more tolerance for distress. That's really the key, not just here, but in self-regulation in general. Your brain is of course a factor. You're using it right now to take in these ideas. But it's not just the brain.

blocks.h: Find what brings you to safety

blocks.p: They asked how to stop or slow the reaction. For this person in particular, I have no idea. For you in particular, I have no idea. But here's what I'd ask you to reflect on: what helps bring you to a baseline?

By baseline, I don't mean your home away from home, the defensive state you're in more often than not. I mean: describe what it feels like for you to be calm, or self-regulated, or in your body, or in the present moment. Maybe you don't know what that's like. That's okay for now. Remember a time when you did feel that way. What does it feel like? Then, mentally, or even on paper if you want, create a map of what it looks like and how to get there.

You need some familiarity with what brings you to safety, especially from a sympathetic fight state. What helps you climb your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) up into your safety state? That's where we want parenting to come from, not from a dominant, defensive state.

For me, if I'm in a more aggressive, frustrated place, I need to shut up, I need to breathe, and I need space. That does it for me. And when I do that, I remind myself how much I love my kids. That's top-down, a thought that can help me change my state. I remind myself that getting angry and not climbing my ladder in that moment isn't going to help. It makes things worse. Usually it's one deep breath, or one slow breath on the way out. Sometimes I close my eyes. That's usually enough for me to say, "Okay," come back, and parent more effectively.

So what helps you self-regulate through your fight energy? If you don't know the answer, that's where you start. Be curious. What helps me climb my polyvagal ladder in general? And what helps me deal with, or climb out of, or feel more effectively, my fight energy?

Don't even worry about changing it. Allow it to be there, but anchor yourself in safety. Even if you're in that aggressive fight state, that's not a bad thing, as long as you're anchored in safety and it's under control. So you might focus on what helps you stay in your body and not get overwhelmed by those defensive states.

Once you know what brings you to safety, you can become curious about what state you're in and what helps you climb out of it. But just identifying what helps you come to safety is always a good place to start, honestly.

blocks.h: Helping the rest of your family

blocks.p: The last part of the question was: "How do I help my husband and daughter do the same?" How do you help them stop or slow the cycle of anger and dysregulation?
The answer is to be self-regulated first. You can't make them stop. That's out of your control. But you can absolutely be self-regulated, if not right now, then eventually.

In my opinion, generational trauma stops when someone is self-regulated enough, and then refuses to continue the patterns that lead to more generational trauma. The teenagers I worked with could see these dynamics in real time, and through therapy they could say, "I don't want to do this to my own kids. This stops with me." That's something I heard from my teen clients a lot. They realized that when they're self-regulated, that's when they can make the best decisions possible, and that will directly impact their own kids in the future.
I'd encourage every single one of us to be that person. But that only comes from doing your own self-regulation growth practice, your own work. It has to come from you, not from anybody else.

blocks.h3: Kids learn from what you model

blocks.p: Your kids will see you doing that, and they'll learn from it. Not so much from watching you practice, though maybe they will. It's more that they'll see you modeling appropriate behavior that comes from your own self-regulation, and they'll feed off that. Kids need to see appropriate modeling of what we want from them, not just hear what we say we want.

They'll learn far better from what you model than from what you say. If you tell them not to swear, but you swear up a storm, don't be surprised if they swear. If you tell them not to hit, but you spank them at home, don't be surprised. They'll learn it from your modeling, good or bad. That's extremely important, and I'd recommend your modeling come from a well-regulated state, from having access to your safety state.
On top of that, if you're able to self-regulate, it might bleed over to your kids and to anybody else in your home. That's co-regulation.

blocks.h3: It's not on you to fix everyone

blocks.p: Just you being self-regulated doesn't solve everything. I know. I get it. And it's not up to you to fix your spouse or anybody else in your life. You're absolutely right. But it is up to you, as a parent, to be a part of fixing the system you're a part of, and that has to start with you.

Ideally, it's a tandem: the two of you working together to address the system of the family. Absolutely. But I don't know if that's possible in your life, and you may have to start with just you. Or the other person may think they're part of the solution when they aren't. We can't coerce people. We can't fix them. We can't tell them how to be. We don't control other people. We can only control, or seemingly control, ourselves.

So I'd start with yourself. That self-regulation will affect other people. It will. I have no idea what that looks like for you, and I'm not saying it'll fix life's problems. But that has to be where you start. You're a part of the system, and you're a parent in the home. That's absolutely your responsibility, and it's something you get to embrace.
